message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This bid is unusual in that it is not based on assumptions about demand: we tested the exact opening pattern at Ashgrove before asking for a penny, and measured the results hour by hour. The pilot showed strong uptake, with evening visits running close to daytime levels and Sunday sessions very popular with families, and new memberships up by about two-thirds on the year before. That gives Members real local evidence that the hours will be used. The costing is equally careful. Staffing is built up from first principles, hours times staff times weeks times branches at the correct graded rate with on-costs, and utilities are taken from actual pilot spend rather than estimates, all of which sums to £174,000. We also looked seriously at the cheaper self-service alternative and explain why it would cost more once building works are included. I am confident this is a well-tested, carefully costed proposal that delivers on the Council Plan.
</author>

<document>
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.
</document>
response:
## Verdict

The proposal is worth funding in some form. The Ashgrove pilot is real local evidence, and the Sunday results in particular are strong. But four things in the bid need correcting before it goes to Members:

1. **The costs sum to £164,000, not £174,000.**
2. **Evening use was well below daytime use, not "close to" it.** Evening visits ran at about 40% of the daytime rate.
3. **The value-for-money figure applies Ashgrove's rates to all five branches,** even though the bid says Ashgrove is the busiest.
4. **The self-service alternative costs more only for about the first three and a half years.**

The pilot data also suggest a better-targeted option than the one proposed.

## What the bid gets right

- **The pilot tested the exact proposed pattern** and recorded use slot by slot. That is better evidence than most growth bids have.
- **The staffing hours are calculated correctly:** 10 hours × 2 staff × 50 weeks × 5 branches = 5,000 hours, and at £24.80 an hour that is £124,000.
- **The visit estimate reproduces from the pilot data.** Each branch would gain 6 evening hours × 21 visits plus 4 Sunday hours × 52 visits, which is 334 visits a week. Over 50 weeks and 5 branches that is about 83,500 visits.
- **The new-membership figure is accurate.** 690 → 1,140 is +65%, so "about two-thirds" is fair.
- **Utilities are probably overstated, which is the cautious direction.** The pilot ran from October to March, when heating and lighting costs peak. Scaling those months up to a full year likely overstates the true annual cost.

## 1. The total is £10,000 too high

The three items in Table 2 add up to £164,000:

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| Staffing | £124,000 |
| Utilities and caretaking | £32,500 |
| Self-service kiosk upgrades | £7,500 |
| **Sum of items** | **£164,000** |
| Stated total | £174,000 |

Either an item is missing from the table or the total is wrong. This needs resolving before the bid goes to Members, because it is the figure they will vote on.

## 2. Evening demand was much weaker than the bid says

Weekday daytime visits averaged about 53 an hour: 3 hours at 46 plus 5 hours at 58, spread over 8 hours. Evening visits averaged 21 an hour, about **40% of the daytime rate**. Section 3, the Conclusion and your covering description all say evening use was "close to" daytime levels. The table doesn't support that.

**Sunday was the strong result,** at 52 visits an hour, close to the daytime rate.

Looking at cost per visit for each slot, using the bid's own cost basis, shows the difference clearly:

| Slot | Weekly cost per branch | Weekly visits | Cost per visit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tue/Thu evenings (6 hrs) | ~£394 | 126 | ~£3.10 |
| Sunday (4 hrs) | ~£262 | 208 | ~£1.25 |

Each slot's cost combines staffing at £24.80 an hour with a per-hour share of utilities and kiosks. Sunday is probably somewhat dearer than shown, because the blended staff rate spreads the Sunday enhancement across evening hours too. The gap would still be large.

So even at Ashgrove, the busiest branch, evening opening costs close to the borough's average of £3.40 per visit.

The Council Plan's target group is working-age adults. The pilot data don't show who used the evening sessions. Age data for evening users and for new members would show whether the extension reaches that group.

## 3. Value for money rests on the busiest branch

The figure of 84,000 visits at around £2 each assumes all five branches match Ashgrove's pilot rates. The bid itself says Ashgrove is the busiest branch and the others may see less demand (section 7). The two statements are inconsistent.

The figure also needs two corrections:
- **Displacement.** Some "additional" visits will be people moving from Saturday or weekday visits. The bid should compare Ashgrove's *total* weekly visits during the pilot with the same months a year earlier.
- **Marginal against average cost.** £2 is the extra cost of the new hours. £3.40 is the borough's average cost, which includes buildings and overheads. Marginal cost will naturally come out lower, so this is not a like-for-like comparison.

**Sensitivity:** if the other four branches see half Ashgrove's use, total extra visits fall to about 50,000. The cost per visit then rises to about £3.30, or £3.50 if the total really is £174,000. That is roughly the borough average, before allowing for any displacement.

The membership rise has the same weakness, because there is no comparison group. Branches that didn't extend their hours over the same period would show how much of the 65% came from the new hours.

## 4. Self-service is cheaper after about three and a half years

The bid says self-service would cut staffing by about two-thirds. Building works would cost £60,000 per branch:

- **Annual saving:** two-thirds of £124,000 ≈ £83,000 a year.
- **One-off cost:** 5 × £60,000 = £300,000, which is capital.
- **Breakeven:** about **3.6 years**. After that, self-service is cheaper.

Your covering note says self-service "would cost more once building works are included". That is true only over a short horizon. The fair comparison also takes account of:
- **Capital and revenue budgets.** These are funded differently, so £300,000 of capital is not directly equivalent to £300,000 of revenue.
- **The insurers' estimate.** It may be lower for branches that already have CCTV.

The bid's stronger argument is the second one: self-service can't host the job club or family sessions.

That argument points to a **hybrid** option. Staff the Thursday evening (job club) and the Sunday (family sessions), and use self-service or no extra opening for Tuesday evening. The bid should cost this.

## 5. Smaller points

- **Pilot length.** The Conclusion calls it a "twelve-month pilot". It ran from October 2025 to March 2026, which is six months.
- **Kiosk upgrades.** It is unclear why staffed opening needs kiosk upgrades. "Upgrades" sounds like a capital cost, but the line is described as a maintenance contract, which is a revenue cost.
- **Staff rate.** The breakdown should show the base rate, the 28% on-costs and the Sunday enhancement separately. Two further items should be confirmed:
  - whether staff time for opening and closing up is included;
  - whether evening work attracts an unsocial-hours enhancement.
- **The six-month review.** It needs a stated threshold, such as a minimum number of visits per hour, and a stated consequence if a branch falls short. Otherwise it isn't a real check.

## Suggested approach for Members

The pilot's evidence is strongest for Sunday opening, and for one staffed evening built around the job club. A bid that:

- funds Sunday opening at all five branches, with one staffed evening at the busiest branches;
- uses the corrected total and branch-specific demand estimates;
- reports net, not gross, extra visits;
- states review criteria in advance;

would cost less than the current request and would be easier to defend. It would also leave Tuesday evenings for a later phase, if the six-month data support them.
